BIG jump in Chinese state-owned refinery run rates following a very slow Hormuz recovery.

State-owned refinery run rates are one of the two most important high frequency indicators of Chinese crude demand alongside tanker tracked crude imports.

This recovery in state-owned runs is currently bigger than the tentative recovery in crude imports, and represents real crude consumption. These run rates, if sustained, will start drawing Chinese crude stocks much faster absent a sharper and durable recovery in crude imports.

Sure my buddy, that's a completely viable scenario. If a pump station along the EW pipeline took a hit, it could easily trigger a flaring event at Abqaiq. That's exactly why I'm weighing options across the board.

Here is the quick breakdown. Raw feed from eastern fields moves into Abqaiq for processing and stabilization, before heading down the EW line to Yanbu.

When a mid route pump station trips, crude throughput stops dead. Pipeline pressure spikes, backing up the exit route at Abqaiq almost instantly.

You can't just throttle incoming upstream crude to zero on a dime, so trapped gas and crude build up inside the processing towers and separators, driving pressure to dangerous levels.

To prevent disaster, automated safety systems trip, immediately diverting trapped off spec gases and volatile liquids to the flare stack to depressurize. Burning through that excess inventory generates a massive flaring event.

Without knowing the exact root cause, I'm holding off on calling it either way. My gut tells me it's practically a 50/50 split right now.

That said finding the flare stack coordinates at Abqaiq takes about 3 minutes. The FinTwit noise merchants pushing doomsday narratives without even doing that bare minimum deserve an instant mute.

Optical satellite imagery of Abqaiq from 5 hours ago. Flames and smoke are showing up at 25.927944° N, 49.698500° E, adjacent to the oil processing facility.

Along with the long shadows, you can see a thick pipe rack extending from the main processing plant on the left. Given the distance from the plant, it appears to be a flare stack.

Looking back through historical satellite passes, this flare stack hasn't flared once all month, making today's flaring event the first recorded instance in July.

Since there could be room for confusion, it seems necessary to approach this with some caution.
